A spray of exhaled breath reveals the tusked gray head of a rauka rising from the brackish water of a river delta. Th is territorial omnivore 
glares over the tumultuous water with beady eyes as its thick jowls clench, chewing the river grass it had swam below to gather. Roaming 
in slow moving herds of dozens of individuals, these aggressive mammals often clear out large expanses of the river mouth from any 
competing creatures, as most do not want to contend with the shearing tusks that twist out from their blunt heads, capable of goring 
and puncturing both hide and thick shell with ease. Th ough aquatic, they have been known to attack any terrestrial aggressors with a 
surprisingly violent charge, erupting onto the beach in short bursts, their strong forelimbs pulling their heavy bulk into a lethal range.

Encountering As the aquatic beasts spend most of their time 
digging up the river floor for aquatic plants and clams, rising 
only periodically to heave in great breaths of air, discovering 
where they roam takes a keen eye as they will often keep far 
below the surface. For those willing to pursue the drove out in 
the waters, they will often be met with an aggressive, tusked 
response by their large males.
Thick blubber does more than protect 
the rauka from the cold, it guards 
their vital organs from predators and 
the rival violence of their own kind
